newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong welcomes Tung's choice of officials.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong welcomes Tung's choice of officials.

text.p: Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa won praise on Friday for reappointing the territory's top officials to their positions in his post-colonial administration.
"His team offers stability and continuity at a crucial time in the territory's history," the South China Morning Post said.
Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, will revert to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.
Beijing has promised the territory of 6.4 million that it would have considerable autonomy and keep its capitalistic way of life intact for 50 years after the sovereignty transfer.
But concerns have been raised recently whether China will keep its pledge after making plans to roll back parts of Hong Kong's democracy and civil liberties laws upon the handover.

Tung's appointment of his team of officials had been viewed as an indicator of how Hong Kong would be run under China. Any major reshuffle would have sent a shock wave to the jittery territory, a day after the death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.

Hong Kong's popular and influential Chief Secretary Anson Chan, deputy to departing British Governor Chris Patten, would serve as Tung's number two when Hong Kong reverts to China later this year. Her post will be renamed Administrative Secretary.

Financial Secretary Donald Tsang would remain in his position as Hong Kong's top economic policy planner. His future was one time in doubt after he made strong comments about China's policy on Hong Kong.
The only changes were the appointment of prominent lawyer Elsie Leung as Secretary for Justice and of civil servant Lily Yam as Commissioner against Corruption.
Leung will replace Attorney General Jeremy Mathews, an expatriate ineligible to remain in his post, while Yam will replace Michael Leung, who will retire in March.
"Mr Tung's announcement will help immeasurably in dispelling some of the gloomy speculation of recent weeks," the Hong Kong Standard said.
"It will also give the lie to the Doubting Thomases in our midst who have been inducing uncertainty and uneasiness here by claiming that China does not keep its word," the newspaper said.
Academic Michael DeGolyer, director of the long-term 1997 transition project studying the handover, said it was a wise move to ensure stability and prosperity.
"One thing we can certainly count on is that with no changes in personnel, with no changes in responsibility, the idea of continuity... is certainly borne out," DeGolyer said.
The Shanghai-born shipping tycoon's choices were also welcomed by British Governor Chris Patten.

"I have been most fortunate during my time as governor to be supported by an outstanding civil service, and I am pleased that Mr Tung Chee-hwa will continue to be served by an excellent team of senior officals," Patten said in a statement on Thursday.

The outgoing British colonial administration had been urging Tung to make as few changes as possible in the ranks of top civil servants, who hold positions akin to cabinet ministers in Britain and wield considerable power.
